title: Which fruits are highest in vitamin C?

seo.title: Fruits highest in vitamin C: a per-100-g ranking
seo.meta_description: Oranges do not top the list. Guava, black currants and kiwi can provide substantially more vitamin C per 100 g. Compare amounts and realistic servings.
seo.search_intent: Compare fruits highest in vitamin C per 100 g and translate the ranking into normal serving sizes.

excerpt: Orange is a good vitamin C source, but it is not the highest. Approximate references per 100 g put guava around 228 mg, black currants around 180 mg, green kiwi near 90 mg, papaya about 60 mg, strawberries about 59 mg and orange around 50 mg. Variety, ripeness and storage can shift the actual amount.
content_html:
Orange has become the cultural symbol of vitamin C, but the actual ranking is much broader. Several fruits provide two, three or even four times as much vitamin C per 100 g.

A per-100-gram comparison

Vitamin C rankings depend heavily on whether the comparison uses equal weight or normal portions. Guava, kiwi, strawberries, citrus, papaya, and several other fruits can all contribute meaningful amounts, but a tiny serving of a concentrated fruit may provide less vitamin C than a larger serving of a more familiar one. That is why per-100-gram tables are useful for comparison but not a complete eating guide. The amount you actually place in a bowl matters just as much as the ranking position.

For a fair comparison, the values below use raw fruit references from food-composition databases. They are approximate: cultivar, ripeness, time after harvest and storage all change the actual content.

FruitApproximate vitamin C
Guava228 mg/100 g
Black currants180 mg/100 g
Green kiwifruit90–95 mg/100 g
Papaya~60 mg/100 g
Strawberries~59 mg/100 g
Orange~50–55 mg/100 g
Grapefruit~30–35 mg/100 g

Guava is the standout: 100 g can provide more than four times the vitamin C of 100 g of orange. Green kiwi also clearly exceeds orange on a weight-for-weight basis.

A serving changes the picture

Ripeness, storage, and cutting can shift vitamin C content because the vitamin is sensitive to oxygen and time. A fresh fruit eaten soon after cutting generally preserves more than fruit left exposed for many hours. Freezing can retain a substantial amount because it slows reactions, while long warm storage tends to be less favorable. These changes do not turn fruit into a poor food; they simply explain why laboratory values and the amount on your plate are never perfectly fixed.

People do not always eat exactly 100 g. NIH lists about 70 mg vitamin C in one medium orange and about 64 mg in one medium kiwi. The per-100-g gap narrows because the orange is usually a larger piece of fruit.

A 150 g serving of strawberries would provide roughly 85–90 mg, even though strawberries rank below kiwi per 100 g.

Vitamin C is sensitive to storage and heat

A useful strategy is to spread vitamin-C-rich foods through ordinary meals rather than chasing a single champion. Berries at breakfast, kiwi as a snack, citrus with lunch, or papaya in a fruit bowl all count. Vegetables such as peppers and broccoli can contribute too, which means fruit does not have to carry the entire job. Variety also brings different fibers, carotenoids, polyphenols, potassium, and flavors that a one-number ranking cannot capture.

Vitamin C is water-soluble and can decline during prolonged storage and cooking. Fresh fruit is usually eaten raw, so cooking loss is less relevant, but storage time and handling still matter.

Juice is not an exact substitute for whole fruit when the goal is a balanced eating pattern. It can provide vitamin C, but it usually contains less fiber per serving and is easy to drink quickly. Whole kiwi, berries, citrus segments, guava, or papaya combine vitamin C with chewing, water, and intact plant structure. If juice is used, it makes more sense to see it as one option among several rather than as the necessary way to reach a vitamin C target.

You do not need to chase the number-one fruit

Labels and nutrition databases can also differ because cultivars, growing conditions, and analytical methods vary. Treat the listed figure as a practical estimate rather than a guarantee that every orange or kiwi contains exactly that amount. For everyday decisions, the bigger distinction is between regularly eating fresh produce and rarely doing so. A fruit that you enjoy and eat often can be more useful nutritionally than a higher-ranked option that stays uneaten in the refrigerator.

NIH lists adult recommendations of 75 mg/day for women and 90 mg/day for men, with higher needs for people who smoke. A normal variety of fruits and vegetables can readily contribute those amounts.

The useful lesson is that citrus, kiwi, strawberries, papaya, guava and many other fruits all contribute meaningfully. Orange deserves its reputation as a good source, just not a monopoly on vitamin C.

faq.question: Which fruit has the most vitamin C?
faq.answer: Among familiar fruits, guava is exceptionally high at about 228 mg/100 g. Less common species can be even higher, so there is no absolute closed ranking for every fruit in the world.

faq.question: Does kiwi have more vitamin C than orange?
faq.answer: Per 100 g, yes: green kiwi is around 90–95 mg versus roughly 50–55 mg for orange. Per piece, the gap narrows because an orange is usually larger.

faq.question: Are strawberries high in vitamin C?
faq.answer: Yes. They provide about 59 mg/100 g, similar to or slightly more than orange by the same weight.
